I've been farming this same land in Quzhou for fifty years. My body knows the seasons better than any calendar. Six mu isn't much, but it's mine, and I know every patch of it.

My wheat and maize share the same four mu — that's how I've always done it here. Plant wheat in October after the summer maize comes off, harvest it in June, then get the maize back in within the week. The other two mu I keep for cotton. Cotton is hard work, and my sons keep telling me to drop it, but I've grown cotton my whole life and the price is decent when it comes in.

For wheat, I'll use the improved variety from the county seed station — not the old seed I saved myself, those yields dropped off years ago. I'll put down compound fertilizer when I plant and push another round of urea when it greens up in March. Three irrigations: the winter water in December to help it survive the cold, jointing water in April, and one more at heading. Two pesticide sprays — one for powdery mildew in spring, one for aphids. I rotary till, I can't manage deep ploughing alone anymore.

Maize goes in right after wheat harvest, direct sow, no tillage — the ground is already worked and I need speed. Hybrid seed, that's been standard for twenty years now. Two irrigations unless the summer rains are good. Maize doesn't need much from me.

Cotton I'll rotary till in April before transplanting. It needs the most attention — aphids, bollworms, I'll spray five times through the season. Four irrigations, especially when it's setting bolls in August. I've learned not to overwater cotton or it gets too vegetative.
